network.tdh.impl.metadataDescription: The Rust core, the Rust and Python references, program B, the Lean model and 6529.io’s backend: how each was written, which conformance vectors it passes, and how they are checked against each other.
network.tdh.impl.title: Implementations
network.tdh.impl.lede: TDH-v1 is one written rule and several programs written separately from it. They run the same test cases and are compared with each other, so a mistake in one shows up as a difference in another.
network.tdh.impl.programs.title: The programs
network.tdh.impl.rust.language: Rust, standard library only, integers only
network.tdh.impl.rust.writtenFrom: Ported from the Rust reference and made into a library, with no rule, arithmetic or decoding code changed. Every ported file is pinned by its hash, and a change to a rule must first be made in P26 and the references.
network.tdh.impl.rust.runsIn: 6529’s daily comparison, scheduled every day since October 16, 2026; 6529.io, from the cutover; every validator, once validators run; proof program A, being built
network.tdh.impl.rust.conformance: All 89 vectors (1,253 checks), at P26 f840096, on the validator’s development branch (30bf8f9, October 16, 2026). The build the daily comparison runs is the one each day’s page names; the later rounds change no value of the October 11, 2026 cycle (P26 §13).
network.tdh.impl.rust.speed: 0.6 s on one core to compute, as measured on the Rust reference it is ported from; inside the validator’s own run on October 15, the TDH-v1 step took 1.7 s on Linux and 5.7 s on Windows. A whole daily run also reads Ethereum and links its block headers, which takes minutes; each day’s page shows its run time
network.tdh.impl.programB.language: Rust, standard library plus a pinned Keccak crate, integers only
network.tdh.impl.programB.writtenFrom: The specifications, the vector files and the design record, in a separate clean room, without opening any other implementation’s code: never the Rust core, the Rust reference or any Python file. It ran the Python reference’s vector runner only as a black box.
network.tdh.impl.programB.runsIn: Proof program B, being built; and, as decided, every validator’s built-in second check before it signs (D125). Not yet inside the validator.
network.tdh.impl.programB.conformance: All 89 vectors, at P26 f840096, on the validator’s development branch (30bf8f9, October 16, 2026); 1,184 checks by its own count
network.tdh.impl.programB.speed: Not measured: no full-day time is recorded for it yet
network.tdh.impl.python.language: Python 3.10 or later, standard library only, no floating point
network.tdh.impl.python.writtenFrom: Written alongside P26 as its reference
network.tdh.impl.python.runsIn: 6529’s daily comparison, scheduled every day since October 16, 2026; any validator, as an optional third check (D125)
network.tdh.impl.python.conformance: All 89 vectors (1,257 checks), at P26 f840096. The daily comparison runs the 6529chain build each day’s page names
network.tdh.impl.python.speed: 4.3 s for the whole cycle (P52 §3.4); in the daily run, on the Rust run’s input, each day’s page gives its time
network.tdh.impl.backend.conformance: Not a TDH-v1 implementation: the specification lists where it differs and its issues, measured by replay and by the daily comparison
network.tdh.impl.written.title: How each was written
network.tdh.impl.written.body: The Python reference came first, written with the specification. The Rust reference was then written in a clean room from P26 and its vectors, without opening the Python, and listed 23 places where it had to choose; P26 now states a rule for each.
network.tdh.impl.written.body2: The Rust reference became the validators’ Rust core with no rule changed. Program B was written later, in a separate clean room, without opening any other implementation’s code; it found that the first netting rule let steps inside a transaction change holdings, and P26 made netting uniform the same day (vectors 45 to 47).
network.tdh.impl.lineage.title: Where each implementation came from
network.tdh.impl.lineage.desc: P26 is the root. The Python reference was written with it. The Rust reference was written from P26, its vectors, the reference README and the documents P26 cites, without reading the Python, and was ported into the Rust core with no rule changed. Program B was written from the specifications, the vectors and the design record, without opening any other implementation’s code. The Lean model was written from P26. The old backend is replaced by the Rust core at the cutover.
network.tdh.impl.where.title: Where each runs, and which checks cover it
network.tdh.impl.checked.title: How they are checked
network.tdh.impl.checked.vectors.title: Conformance vectors.
network.tdh.impl.checked.vectors.body: 89 small cases, each with the exact values the rule must produce: zero holdings, editions, transfers inside one block, transaction netting, consolidation carry, burns, FirstGM, floors, boost tiers, rounding ties, malformed events, the input rules made explicit on October 15 and 16, and inputs that must produce no result. A program conforms when it reproduces every one.
network.tdh.impl.checked.replays.title: Differential replays.
network.tdh.impl.checked.replays.body: Whole days run through more than one implementation and compared with 6529.io’s published values. With D131’s netting, the 2026-10-11 replay reproduces all 10,280 identities and 11,130 wallets; before netting it reproduced 10,278, and the two others were explained (DEV-2).
network.tdh.impl.checked.dual.title: The dual run in every validator.
network.tdh.impl.checked.dual.body: Before it signs, a validator is to compute TDH with the Rust core and with program B; if they disagree on any value, it does not sign and raises an alarm. The Python reference is an optional third check. This is decided (D125, P53 §4.5) but not yet built in: program B does not run inside the validator yet.
network.tdh.impl.checked.daily.title: The daily comparison.
network.tdh.impl.checked.daily.body: 6529 runs the Rust core and the Python reference beside 6529.io’s backend and publishes the three results. Days are compared from October 14, 2026; the scheduled job runs every day since October 16, and October 14 and 15 were first computed on October 15, then recomputed on October 16. Each day’s file says when it was written and by which builds. The Python run reads the Rust run’s own input, after checking its hash, so the two compare computation, not reading Ethereum. The comparison is a separate tool, three_way.py, in the validator code.
network.tdh.impl.checked.proofs.title: Proofs.
network.tdh.impl.checked.proofs.body: Programs A and B are being built to prove each day’s result from Ethereum’s own history in two different zero-knowledge virtual machines; a minimal Ethereum contract that records proven results is being built and tested against a fork of Ethereum mainnet, and nothing is deployed until the owner approves.
network.tdh.impl.checked.after: After the cutover, 6529.io runs the Rust core itself, so comparing the two no longer tests the computation, only its publication. The independent check of the published day is then the Python reference, in the daily comparison; program B joins once it runs inside validators (D125, planned).

network.tdh.impl.anatomy.title: Inside one vector
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.intro: Vector 36: one transaction sends copies of two Memes to a marketplace and back, and one copy goes on to a buyer. Its addresses and transactions are synthetic. A program reads the transfers and the cycle, and must produce exactly the expected values.
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.derivationBody: All five movements are in one transaction, so each token’s movements are netted (P26 §7.1). Meme 1: wallet A and the marketplace W each net zero, so nothing moves and A keeps its 100- and 40-day-old copies. Meme 2: A nets −1, W nets 0 and buyer B +1, so one copy goes from A to B: A’s last copy, 60 days old, which B receives fresh, 5 days before the snapshot. Without netting, A’s copies would have left and come back fresh: 285 whole days instead of 560.
network.tdh.impl.v.36-erc1155-send-and-r: Several copies out to a marketplace and back, one sold on
network.tdh.impl.v.37-pass-through-clust: A to W to C in one transaction acts as A to C, with age carried inside an identity
network.tdh.impl.v.38-pairing-order: Two senders and two receivers out of address order: paired in address order
network.tdh.impl.v.39-mint-forwarded: A mint passed on inside the transaction, and a zero-amount creation mint
network.tdh.impl.v.40-mint-and-burn-in-o: Minted and burned in one transaction: a burn to the zero address credits nobody, one to 0x…dead credits the sink; the mints still count in the editions
network.tdh.impl.v.41-firstgm-netting: Netting inside the FirstGM burn transaction
network.tdh.impl.v.42-batch-repeated-id: Batch events with a repeated id, out and back
network.tdh.impl.v.43-different-transact: Not netted: two transactions of one block, and one transaction index in two blocks
network.tdh.impl.v.44-invalid-underflow-: No result: an underflow before netting, though the transaction nets to zero
network.tdh.impl.v.45-inserted-round-tri: A round trip inserted before a transaction’s transfers: every value stays the same
network.tdh.impl.v.46-round-trip-before-: A round trip before a seller’s sale does not make it the first sender
network.tdh.impl.v.47-sink-round-trip: A round trip through 0x…dead nets out: nothing burned or credited

network.tdh.impl.v.49-invalid-transactio: No result: one transaction’s transfers carry two timestamps

network.tdh.impl.checked.difftest.title: Differential tests across four programs.
network.tdh.impl.checked.difftest.body: On October 15 and 16, five rounds of generated cycles ran through the Lean model, the Python reference, the Rust core and program B. Each round’s findings were settled in P26 and pinned by new vectors, except E13, from the fifth round, which is open for the vector format. In CI, 6529chain runs 1,000 seeded random inputs through Lean, Python and the Rust reference on every change, and since the fourth round the validator’s CI runs the Rust core against program B.

network.tdh.impl.programs.intro: Three programs written separately (the Python reference, the Rust reference and program B), the Rust core ported from the Rust reference, and the Lean model compute TDH-v1. Every day 6529.io’s current backend is compared record by record with the Rust core, and the Rust core with the Python reference. The Rust core and program B are to be published with the validator code (D116); the references and the Lean model are in 6529’s private design repository.
network.tdh.impl.speedShort.rust: 0.6 s alone; 1.7 s (Linux) to 5.7 s (Windows) inside the validator’s run
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.legend: A is wallet 0x…a1, W a marketplace at 0x…ee and B the buyer at 0x…b2. T, the snapshot block’s time, is 1,791,676,799 (2026-10-10 23:59:59 UTC); each transfer’s age is the whole days between its block’s time and T. The vector’s own registry lists one season, starting at Meme 1.
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.boostBody: Boost: the vector’s registry has one season, which is therefore the current season and pays nothing. A holds both eligible Memes, 5 and 3 copies, so 3 full sets: 1.00 plus the extra-set bonus ADD(3) = 0.082645, rounded to 1.08 (boost_c 108, in cents). B holds one Meme only: 1.00.

network.tdh.impl.byHand.summary: Three more vectors to check by hand: 04, 06 and 23
network.tdh.impl.byHand.intro: Restated in full from their files at P26 f840096, like vector 36: every address, transaction and token is synthetic. A transfer’s position is its block, transaction index and log index; its days are the whole days before the vector’s T (a + marks part of a day more); a record that is not listed is not checked.
network.tdh.impl.byHand.setting: Wallets: {wallets}. The vector’s registry starts seasons at Memes {seasons}. T, the snapshot block’s time, is {time} ({date} 23:59:59 UTC).
network.tdh.impl.byHand.links: Consolidation registrations, use case 999 for The Memes:
network.tdh.impl.byHand.04.title: Last in, first out
network.tdh.impl.byHand.04.why: A’s stack of Meme 1 is [T−30d, T−30d, T−20d], and the sale removes the last entry, T−20d: A keeps two copies of 30 days (raw 60), and B’s copy starts fresh at T−10d. One Meme with 3 minted, so H = E = 3 and the rate is 1.00. A holds two full sets: 1.00 + ADD(2) = 1.05, and 60 × 1.05 = 63. B holds one set, and the vector’s only season is the current one: 1.00.
network.tdh.impl.byHand.06.title: Age carried inside an identity
network.tdh.impl.byHand.06.why: A and B confirm their link at block 1101, after B sent its copy to A at block 1004. TDH-v1 applies the grouping at B to the whole history, so the copy keeps B’s acquisition time: A’s stack is [T−100d, T−80d, T−200d], raw 380. One Meme with 3 minted: rate 1.00. The identity holds three sets: 1.00 + ADD(3) = 1.082645, rounded to 1.08, and 380 × 1.08 = 410.4, rounded to 410.
network.tdh.impl.byHand.23.title: Identity sums and their rounding
network.tdh.impl.byHand.23.why: Editions are 5, 4, 5 and 5, so H = 5 and Meme 2’s rate is 1.25. Seasons start at Memes 1 and 4: season 1 (Memes 1 to 3) is boostable, season 2 is current. Neither A nor B holds every Meme (each gets Nakamoto’s +0.01: 1.01), but their identity does: one full set, so season 1 pays, 1.05. Meme 2: each wallet’s base is (125 × 1 + 50) div 100 = 1, so the identity’s is 2, not 3 from its merged raw days. Meme 4: the identity’s FINAL(20, 105) = 21, where two wallets’ FINAL(10, 105) = 11 would give 22. The identity’s final is 26 + 2 + 11 + 21 = 60. Identity P + Q + R: P’s copy of Meme 3, bought at T−100d, moves to Q at T−50d and to R at T−20d, keeping its age both times, so R’s stack is [T−30d, T−100d]; R’s sale at T−5d removes the last entry, the carried copy, and R keeps raw 30.
